title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)


my_state <- "NY"
my_variable <- "B25064_001"


county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)


dim(county_data)

[1] 62  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York      B25064_001     1252    22
2 36003 Allegany County, New York    B25064_001      754    33
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       B25064_001     1436    11
4 36007 Broome County, New York      B25064_001      914    26
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York B25064_001      759    30
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York      B25064_001      895    39


There are 62 rows, and 62 counties in New York state.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York        860    95   11.0 
 2 Schuyler County, New York        858    75    8.74
 3 Greene County, New York          993    79    7.96
 4 Lewis County, New York           821    59    7.19
 5 Orleans County, New York         877    60    6.84
 6 Yates County, New York           802    46    5.74
 7 Wyoming County, New York         782    44    5.63
 8 Cortland County, New York        911    50    5.49
 9 Chenango County, New York        819    44    5.37
10 Livingston County, New York      912    48    5.26


The county with the largest margin of error to it’s estimate, or the least reliable, is Hamilton County. The margin of error to it’s estimate as a percent is 11.05%.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    51
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate           10


When I first kept the margins to < 5% and <10%, the numbers came up as 51 high confidence, 1 low confidence, and 10 moderate confidence. But when I adjusted the cut offs to < 3% and < 10%, the numbers shifted significantly to 27 high confidence, 1 low confidence, and 34 moderate confidence. The shows that there were 24 counties that had a 3-4% margin of error, which is realitively high considering the number of total counties in the state of NY. 

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York        1252     22  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York       754     33   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York         1436     11 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York         914     26  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York    759     30   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York         895     39   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))


county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        381479.
2 Moderate                11         37898.


We are grouping by reliability (in this case either high or moderate), then the number of counties in each category, with the mean of the estimated population for all of the counties in each category. The average population of high-confidence counties is 381,479.14, where moderate counties are 37,898.45. This indicates that the average population for counties with a moderate reliability are significantly lower than counties with a high confidence. This means that the larger the county, the more reliable the numbers are.
The counties in New York state that we know the least about are Hamilton County, Schuyler County, Greene County, Lewis County, Orleans County, Wyoming County, and Yates County. All of these counties have Moderate (<5%x<15%) percent margin of error for the Gross Median Rent. These are also counties that have smaller estimated population sizes. Because the ACS only collects data from a sample of the population, it makes sense that in counties with smaller estimated population sizes there would be a higher percent margin of error since they are less people to be surveyed. That being said, the majority of the county falls within High Confidence reliability, meaning that their percent margin of error is <5%, and their population size is larger. The average population size for High Confidence counties (n=51) is 381,479.14 while for Moderate counties (n=11) it is 37,898.45. When a state agency allocates funding using my variable (gross median rent), they would be missing a significant portion of the population of the less populous counties. This could fail to consider the reality of the housing affordability crisis in smaller, more rural counties in New York state.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Increase and Widening Income Disparity in Philadelphia 2006-2017
text:
I first pulled 5-year ACS data for 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 for total population, population below poverty level, and medium household income at the census tract level.These are the two most referenced chunks of data in the article. These time periods do not overlap, which is important in preventing any kind of distorted trend. I then found the Census Tracts with the population estimates as zero. These tracts were the same for both 2006-2010 and 2013-2017. Cross referencing with a map, these are areas that are have industrial uses. I chose to remove these tracts from my analysis because even though they have a margin of error, the sample size would be so small it would be highly unreliable. I then calculated the poverty rate, it’s margin of error, and the coefficient of variation for the ACS 2006-2010 and ACS 2013-2017 data. Report how many tracts show a statistically detectable change and how many do not: 
#ACS 2006-2017


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)

acs_10 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    total = "B17001_001",
    below_poverty = "B17001_002",
    medium_HH_income = "B19013_001E"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output =  "wide"
)


#ACS 2013-2017


Show code
acs_17 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    total = "B17001_001",
    below_poverty = "B17001_002",
    medium_HH_income = "B19013_001E"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


#Missing Values


Show code
acs_10 <- acs_10 %>%
  filter(totalE != 0 & !is.na(totalE))

acs_17 <- acs_10 %>%
  filter(totalE != 0 & !is.na(totalE))




Show code
#Poverty Percent and Margin of Error

acs_10 <- acs_10 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_pct = below_povertyE / totalE * 100,
    moe_pct = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE,
      totalE,
      below_povertyM,
      totalM
    )
  )

acs_17 <- acs_17 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_pct = below_povertyE / totalE * 100,
    moe_pct = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE,
      totalE,
      below_povertyM,
      totalM
    )
  )

#Standard Error and Coefficient of Variation

acs_10 <- acs_10 %>%
  mutate(
    se = moe_pct / 1.645,
    cv = (se / poverty_pct) * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "High",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE             ~ "Low"
    )
  )

acs_17 <- acs_17 %>%
  mutate(
    se = moe_pct / 1.645,
    cv = (se / poverty_pct) * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "High",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE             ~ "Low"
    )
  )




Show code
acs_10 <- acs_10 %>%
  mutate(
    se = moe_pct / 1.645,
    cv = (se / poverty_pct) * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "High",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE             ~ "Low"
    )
  )

acs_17 <- acs_17 %>%
  mutate(
    se = moe_pct / 1.645,
    cv = (se / poverty_pct) * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "High",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE             ~ "Low"
    )
  )


#Visualizing Margins of Error


Show code
acs_17 %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, totalE), y = totalE)) +
  geom_col(fill = "orange") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = totalE - totalM, ymax = totalE + totalM), width = 0.3, color = "black") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Census Tracts with the largest margins of error",
    subtitle = "People below the poverty level, ACS 2017 5-year estimates",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Population below poverty level"
  )









#Calculating change over time for poverty and medium household income.


Show code
acs_10_poverty <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    below_poverty = "B17001_002"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output =  "wide"
)


acs_17_poverty <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    below_poverty = "B17001_002"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output =  "wide"
)

#I then joined the two tables together

philly_poverty <- acs_10_poverty %>%
  left_join (
    acs_17_poverty,
    by = "GEOID",
    suffix = c("_2010", "_2017")
  )

#and then calculated the change between the two periods

philly_poverty <- philly_poverty %>%
  mutate (
    change = below_povertyE_2017 - below_povertyE_2010,
    se_1 = below_povertyM_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2 = below_povertyM_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

philly_poverty <- philly_poverty %>%
  filter(below_povertyE_2010 != 0 & !is.na(below_povertyE_2010))

philly_poverty %>%
  count(significant)


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  significant     n
  <lgl>       <int>
1 FALSE         306
2 TRUE           69

  filter(significant) %>%
  mutate(
    NAME_2010 = str_remove(NAME_2010, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    NAME_2017 = str_remove(NAME_2017, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")
  ) %>%

    ),

#Part 3: Adjudicate The article argues that there has been an increase in people living below the poverty level and a widening of wage inequality in Philadelphia between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017. Despite this being true for the estimated values, the article does not take into consideration the statistical uncertainty of the data.
Out of the 306 Census Tracts (I excluded the tracts that were NA), only 69 (23%) of them experienced a change in poverty rates that are statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90 percent confidence level. The increases and decreases in the remaining tracts cannot be used because of the uncertainty. This is also true for the change in medium household income, where out of the 306 Census Tracts, only 78 (25%) are statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90 percent confidence level. Rather that indicating that there has been a change in poverty in Philadelphia between these two time periods, the data simple shows that poverty continues to exist.
#Part 4: Rewrite
A surface-level analysis of the change in poverty level and medium household income in Philadelphia from data taken from the 5-year ACS for 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 indicate that there has been a drastic increase in poverty. However, this data does not take into consideration the margin of error of this data, and therefore the margin of error in the rate of change. That is, only 23% of the poverty data and 25% of the medium household income data show changes that would be considered statistically significant. Despite this uncertainty, the data still indicates that poverty has been and continues to be pervasive in Philadelphia. There has just not been a large signifigant change.

I first pulled 5-year ACS data for 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 for total population, population below poverty level, and medium household income at the census tract level.These are the two most referenced chunks of data in the article. These time periods do not overlap, which is important in preventing any kind of distorted trend. I then found the Census Tracts with the population estimates as zero. These tracts were the same for both 2006-2010 and 2013-2017. Cross referencing with a map, these are areas that are have industrial uses. I chose to remove these tracts from my analysis because even though they have a margin of error, the sample size would be so small it would be highly unreliable. I then calculated the poverty rate, it’s margin of error, and the coefficient of variation for the ACS 2006-2010 and ACS 2013-2017 data. #Part 3: Adjudicate The article argues that there has been an increase in people living below the poverty level and a widening of wage inequality in Philadelphia between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017. Despite this being true for the estimated values, the article does not take into consideration the statistical uncertainty of the data.
Out of the 306 Census Tracts (I excluded the tracts that were NA), only 69 (23%) of them experienced a change in poverty rates that are statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90 percent confidence level. The increases and decreases in the remaining tracts cannot be used because of the uncertainty. This is also true for the change in medium household income, where out of the 306 Census Tracts, only 78 (25%) are statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90 percent confidence level. Rather that indicating that there has been a change in poverty in Philadelphia between these two time periods, the data simple shows that poverty continues to exist.
#Part 4: Rewrite
A surface-level analysis of the change in poverty level and medium household income in Philadelphia from data taken from the 5-year ACS for 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 indicate that there has been a drastic increase in poverty. However, this data does not take into consideration the margin of error of this data, and therefore the margin of error in the rate of change. That is, only 23% of the poverty data and 25% of the medium household income data show changes that would be considered statistically significant. Despite this uncertainty, the data still indicates that poverty has been and continues to be pervasive in Philadelphia. There has just not been a large signifigant change.

Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.

5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.
Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.

The ACS baseline model (m1) performed best, with a CV RMSE of 11.85, indicating the lowest prediction error. The log transformation of affordable housing density did not improve the model, with a CV RMSE of 12.91. This may be because affordable housing density does not have a strong enough relationship with poverty rates to improve predictions beyond the baseline variables. The affordable housing density and per-capita rate model (m2) performed worst, with a CV RMSE of 13.40, suggesting that these additional predictors did not provide enough useful information to improve the model’s accuracy.
Another feature that lowered the CV RMSE the most was the Squared Distance to Empowerment Zone model. This was interesting to me, considering that I tend to believe that a lot of this city-sponsored programs tend to have hollow promises of alleviating poverty and don’t often get to the source of the problem (decades of disinvestment, lack of jobs).
